about.title: Brisbane Premises Liability Claims
about.longDescription: Brisbane is a small city, but its mix of hillside neighborhoods, warehouse-district businesses along Bayshore Boulevard, and retail spots near US-101 means uneven pavement, poorly lit stairwells, and slick loading areas show up more than people expect. If you slipped or tripped on someone else's property in Brisbane, California law generally requires showing the property owner knew or reasonably should have known about the hazard and failed to fix it or warn you. That's why what happens right after your fall matters: photos of the spot, notes on lighting or spills, and a request to preserve any surveillance footage can make a real difference later. LawProactive doesn't practice law or promise outcomes — we simply connect injured Brisbane residents with an independent personal injury attorney who can evaluate the property owner's responsibility and pursue a claim on a contingency basis, meaning there's no fee unless you recover.

whyChoose.title: What Matters in a Brisbane Premises Liability Claim

items.title: Proving the Owner Had Notice
items.desc: California requires showing the property owner knew or should have known about the hazard and didn't fix it or warn you. An attorney can help track down maintenance logs, prior complaints, or inspection records to establish this.

items.title: Preserving Video Before It's Erased
items.desc: Many Brisbane businesses along Bayshore Boulevard and near US-101 run surveillance systems that overwrite footage within days or weeks. Getting a preservation request out quickly can be the difference between having proof and having nothing.

items.title: Understanding Comparative Fault
items.desc: California uses pure comparative fault, so even if you're partly blamed for not seeing a hazard, you can still pursue compensation reduced by your share of fault. An attorney can help push back on unfair fault allocations.

items.question: How long do I have to file a slip and fall claim in Brisbane?
items.answer: Generally, California gives you two years from the date of the fall to file a lawsuit. If the property involved is owned by a government entity — a public sidewalk or a city building, for example — that deadline can be much shorter, sometimes just months. It's best to have this reviewed early so you don't lose your ability to pursue a claim.

items.question: What if the store or property owner says I was watching where I was going?
items.answer: That's a common response, and it relates to California's comparative fault rule. Even if you're found partly at fault, you can still recover damages, just reduced by your percentage of responsibility. An independent attorney can help gather evidence to counter unfair claims about your own carelessness.

items.question: I fell near a business on Bayshore Boulevard — what should I do first?
items.answer: Try to take photos of exactly what caused the fall, note the time and conditions, and ask an employee or manager to document the incident in writing. If there are cameras nearby, request in writing that the footage be preserved, since many systems overwrite recordings quickly. After that, getting a free case review from an independent attorney can help you understand your options.
